analysis.one_liner: Cuts Medicaid, Medicare, and welfare to balance the budget by 2002, while adding a per-child tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to 14 House committees and 8 subcommittees, drew zero cosponsors, and died without any vote when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the House Budget Committee chairman's full package to balance the federal budget by 2002. It capped federal Medicaid payments, cut Medicare hospital and home-health payments, replaced cash welfare with time-limited block grants, and trimmed federal retirement and veterans benefits. It also added a $300-per-child tax credit, a college tuition deduction, new Medicare screenings, stronger child-support enforcement, spectrum auctions, and several corporate tax increases.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed: families with young children would get a $300-per-child tax credit rising to $500, families could deduct up to $10,000 of college costs, and self-employed people could deduct more health insurance costs. Medicare beneficiaries would gain annual mammography and colorectal screening coverage and elimination of vaccine cost-sharing, and Medicaid states could cover more people. People facing FHA mortgage default would get foreclosure-avoidance help, and single parents would benefit from tougher child-support enforcement. Everyone holding the debt would benefit from the deficit reduction itself.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $300-per-child tax credit for children under 13, rising to $500 after 1998, phased down for incomes of $60,000 and above.
Allows a deduction of up to $10,000 for qualified higher education expenses, with the limit reduced at higher incomes.
Adds Medicare coverage of annual mammography for women over 49 and colorectal screening, waives cost-sharing for mammography, and eliminates coinsurance and deductibles for hepatitis B vaccine.
Gives states new options to extend Medicaid coverage to additional people and to offer home- and community-based long-term care without a waiver.

Replaces the AFDC cash welfare program with Temporary Employment Assistance plus a WORK FIRST employment block grant aimed at moving recipients into private-sector jobs, with child care funding prioritized for families moving off assistance.

Strengthens child-support enforcement with a centralized case registry, automated new-hire directory, license suspension, passport denial for arrears over $5,000, and liability for grandparents supporting children of minor parents.
Expands spectrum auctions, requiring the FCC to auction at least 100 megahertz of additional spectrum and to reclaim and auction analog TV spectrum after the digital transition.

Raises revenue from corporations and wealthy individuals, including taxing property of citizens who renounce U.S. citizenship as if sold, requiring registration of corporate tax shelters, and phasing down the Puerto Rico tax credit.

analysis.who_pays: Medicaid beneficiaries would face capped federal funding per enrollee through 2002, shifting cost control to states. Cash welfare would become time-limited, with assistance denied for noncompliance with individual responsibility plans and states allowed to deny aid for children born while a family is on assistance. Hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, and home health agencies would take Medicare payment cuts, some of which could reach patients as reduced access. Federal employees and retirees would pay higher retirement contributions and face delayed cost-of-living adjustments through 2002. Veterans would face extended copayments and capped disability COLAs. Savers would lose the exclusion for short-term vacation-home rental income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid and welfare recipients, hospitals, federal retirees

drawbacks.text: Medicaid would be capped at a per-beneficiary rate of growth for FY1997–2002, so a recession, epidemic, or aging wave would force states to cut eligibility, benefits, or provider rates rather than receive more federal money.

The welfare title replaces AFDC with time-limited assistance, requires individual responsibility plans with benefits denied after a third act of noncompliance, and lets states deny aid to families who have another child while on assistance and to minor parents.

Medicare savings come largely from payment reductions to hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, and home health agencies — including temporary rate freezes and a move to per-episode prospective payment — which providers argued could limit access to care.

Existing TV broadcasters would receive new digital television licenses free, explicitly exempted from the competitive bidding that applies to most other spectrum — a transfer of publicly owned airwaves to incumbent broadcast companies.

Oil and gas companies would get royalty relief, including royalty suspension for seven years on some new deepwater Gulf of Mexico leases, meaning the public receives less for resources taken from federal waters.

Federal retirees and employees would bear higher contributions and delayed COLAs, and veterans would face continued copayments and disability COLAs limited to Social Security's increase through FY2002.

Benefits to families are modest relative to the cuts: the child credit phases out starting at $60,000 of income, and the bill cuts food stamp benefits (minimum allotments, deductions, student earnings) and tightens SSI for disabled children and for people whose disability involves drug or alcohol addiction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The package is a genuine trade rather than a one-sided deal: real middle-class tax relief, new Medicare preventive benefits, and deficit reduction on one side; capped Medicaid funding, time-limited welfare, and Medicare provider payment cuts on the other. Its weakest points are structural — capping federal Medicaid spending per beneficiary transfers all the risk of rising health costs to states and patients, and the free digital TV licenses to incumbent broadcasters simply give away a public asset to a concentrated industry at the same time the bill auctions off everyone else's spectrum. An honest supporter would have to concede that the heaviest burdens fall on the poorest families and the oldest and sickest beneficiaries, while the largest uncontested gains go to broadcasters and deepwater oil producers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to 14 House committees, a few pieces went to subcommittees in February, and then nothing happened — it sat until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 with no markup, no floor vote, and not even one cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kasich introduced the bill on January 26, 1996, marked as introduced 'by request,' and it was referred to the Budget Committee and 13 other committees at once.

Between February 1 and February 9, 1996, portions were referred to subcommittees including Human Resources, Health, Military Readiness, Energy and Power, Health and Environment, Telecommunications and Finance, and Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials.
No committee ever reported the bill and no chamber ever voted on it; all action ends in February 1996, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing passed, Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries, welfare families, federal retirees, and veterans kept the benefit rules in effect at the time, and none of the bill's caps, time limits, or payment cuts took effect. Its middle-class tax credits, new Medicare screenings, and corporate tax increases also never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Safety-net beneficiaries kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. John Kasich
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House as a comprehensive balanced-budget package.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: The bill was introduced 'by request,' the convention for a bill introduced at the President's request, and its 'Middle Class Bill of Rights' tax-credit title matched the proposals Clinton had just put forward in January 1996.

against.name: House committee chairmen of the 14 committees of referral
against.role: Budget, Ways and Means, Commerce, Banking, Judiciary, Agriculture, Education and Workforce, Government Reform, House Oversight, National Security, Veterans' Affairs, Resources, International Relations, and Rules
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; none of the 14 committees or their subcommittees ever reported it, so it never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single sponsor with zero cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan lineup for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would give existing TV stations new digital television licenses free of charge, explicitly exempting them from the auction requirement applied to most spectrum, while delaying any auction of their replacement licenses. This hands a scarce public resource worth billions to incumbent broadcast companies at no charge.

The bill creates a Medicare Part C letting every beneficiary enroll in an HMO, PPO, or provider-sponsored organization, and lets states require Medicaid recipients to enroll in managed care — routing public health dollars through private insurance plans and making them the gatekeepers, while imposing solvency and quality standards on them.

Medicare payment updates would be recalibrated downward, disproportionate-share and indirect-medical-education payments cut, and home health moved to frozen cost limits and then per-episode payment. Lower payments reduce federal spending but risk reduced access for Medicare patients.
Deepwater Gulf of Mexico leases would get royalty relief and seven-year royalty suspensions, so companies pay the public less for oil and gas taken from federal waters.

Thrifts would pay a large one-time special assessment to recapitalize the savings insurance fund, but the bill also caps future assessments, allows hardship installment payments, exempts specified institutions, and requires refunds of fund excesses back to member institutions.

The government-owned uranium enricher would be privatized, receiving federal uranium stockpile transfers, exclusive rights to federal laser-enrichment patents, and tariff exemptions on Russian weapons uranium — with worker protections and national-security licensing conditions attached.
